lessons.title: Inflation, Trade Deficits and the Current Account

children.text: In August 2013, a Morgan Stanley report grouped India with Brazil, Indonesia, South Africa and Turkey as the "Fragile Five," economies too dependent on foreign money to pay their bills. India's current account deficit had hit 4.8% of GDP, and the rupee crashed to a then record low of about 68.85. Fast forward to FY26: the deficit is just 0.6% of GDP, yet the rupee is trading near 95.5. If the deficit is tiny, why is the rupee still weak? To answer that, you need to understand how inflation slowly erodes a currency, and how the current account and capital flows decide whether India earns enough foreign currency to cover what it spends.

body.text: Inflation decides where a currency drifts over years. The balance of payments decides how hard it gets pushed in any given quarter. Watch both, and remember that a small trade gap can still be swamped by capital leaving the country.

children.text: Inflation: The Slow Leak in a Currency's Value

markDefs.definition: Purchasing power parity. The idea that exchange rates should adjust so the same basket of goods costs the same in two countries, once converted into one currency.

children.text: Inflation means each rupee buys less than it used to. If prices in India rise faster than prices in the US, the rupee loses purchasing power faster than the dollar does, and over time it takes more rupees to buy a dollar. This idea is called
purchasing power parity
, or PPP. It is the gravity that pulls exchange rates in the long run.

Worked example: a laptop costs ₹95,500 in India and $1,000 in the US, which matches USD/INR at 95.50. Over the next year, Indian prices rise 5% and US prices rise 2%. The laptop now costs ₹1,00,275 in India and $1,020 in the US. For the prices to stay equal, USD/INR would need to be 1,00,275 ÷ 1,020 = 98.31. The 3 percentage point inflation gap implies USD/INR should rise by about 2.9%.

body.caption: Relative PPP. Notice it has the same shape as the forward rate formula from Chapter 2, with inflation in place of interest rates.

body.title: Five years of inflation gap
body.prompt: USD/INR is 95.50. Suppose Indian inflation runs at 5% a year and US inflation at 2.5% a year for five years. Using relative PPP, what would USD/INR be after five years? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Rate after five years = 95.50 × (1.05 ÷ 1.025)^5 = 95.50 × 1.0244^5 = 95.50 × 1.1281 = 107.73. A 2.5 percentage point inflation gap, compounded, implies about 12.8% more rupees per dollar in five years. That is why even a steady, well-managed rupee tends to drift weaker over long periods.

body.text: PPP is a compass, not a clock. Over a decade, countries with persistently higher inflation almost always see their currencies weaken. Over a month or a quarter, PPP tells you very little, because capital flows, interest rates, oil prices and RBI intervention dominate. Use PPP to understand the long-term drift of the rupee, never to time a trade.

children.text: Trade Deficit vs Current Account: Not the Same Thing

markDefs.definition: A country's net earnings from the rest of the world: trade in goods and services, investment income, and transfers such as remittances. A deficit means it spends more foreign currency than it earns.
Goods imports minus goods exports. Only one part of the current account.

children.text: Headlines love the
merchandise trade deficit
because it comes out every month and is big. But the number that matters for the rupee is the
current account

, which adds India's huge services exports and remittances on top of goods trade, and subtracts interest and dividends paid to foreign investors. India's goods gap is enormous. Its current account gap is small, because services and Indians working abroad fill most of the hole.

body.caption: India's current account, Q1 FY27 (April to June 2026), RBI data

cells: Crude oil, gold, electronics and machinery imports minus goods exports
Software, business services, travel and transport, net
Remittances inflows, minus interest and dividends paid abroad

body.title: Building India's Current Account, Q1 FY27 ($ billion)
Fill the gap
body.prompt: In Q1 FY26, a year earlier, India's merchandise trade deficit was $68.9 billion, net services receipts were $47.9 billion, and the current account deficit was $3.4 billion. What was the net of transfers and investment income, in $ billion?
body.explanation: Current account = goods + services + transfers and income. So minus 3.4 = minus 68.9 + 47.9 + X, which gives X = minus 3.4 + 68.9 minus 47.9 = +17.6. Note: RBI's own breakdown may differ slightly because of rounding and revisions. The point is the structure: goods pull India into deficit, services and remittances pull it back.

body.title: India's Current Account Deficit (% of GDP, negative means surplus)
Why crude oil and gold dominate India's current account

children.text: India imports most of the crude oil it uses, so every sustained rise in oil prices adds billions of dollars to the import bill without India buying a single extra barrel. That is why the rupee usually weakens when Brent crude spikes.

Gold is the other big swing factor. Indian households buy gold for weddings, festivals and savings, and almost all of it is imported. In FY26, gold imports rose 24.1% to $71.98 billion. When gold prices are high and demand stays strong, the current account takes the hit. In the 2013 crisis, the government raised gold import duty and imposed restrictions specifically to protect the rupee.

body.title: What improves the current account?
body.question: Which of these would directly reduce India's current account deficit?
options: A surge in gold imports ahead of the wedding season
Brent crude rising from $85 to $110 a barrel
Indian IT and business services exports growing strongly
A $5 billion inflow from FPIs buying Indian bonds
body.explanation: Higher services exports add to the current account. Gold and crude imports widen the deficit. FPI bond buying brings in dollars too, but it is recorded in the capital account, not the current account, and it can reverse quickly.

children.text: The Other Half: The Capital Account

markDefs.definition: Investment and borrowing flows between a country and the world, such as FDI, FPI, NRI deposits and external commercial borrowings. Called the capital and financial account in official data.
The full record of a country's transactions with the world: the current account plus the capital account, with the balance showing up as a change in forex reserves.

children.text: A current account deficit has to be paid for. The money comes from the
capital account
: foreign companies building factories, FPIs buying shares and bonds, NRIs depositing dollars, and Indian firms borrowing abroad. Together, the two accounts make up the
balance of payments
. If capital inflows exceed the current account deficit, RBI can add to reserves. If they fall short, either the rupee weakens or RBI sells reserves to fill the gap.

body.latex: \text{Current account} + \text{Capital account} + \text{Errors and omissions} = \text{Change in forex reserves}
body.caption: The balance of payments identity

children.text: This solves the puzzle from the start of the lesson. In Q1 FY27, India's current account deficit was only $4.2 billion. But FPIs pulled out a net $9.6 billion in the same quarter, against an inflow of $1.6 billion a year earlier, while net FDI brought in just $6.1 billion. A small trade gap plus fleeing portfolio money still adds up to strong dollar demand. The rupee's weakness in 2026 has far more to do with the capital account than the current account.

body.title: How a current account deficit gets funded

columns.label: Stable funding
points: Foreign direct investment in factories and businesses
Long-term loans with fixed repayment schedules
Hard to pull out quickly in a panic

columns.label: Hot money
points: FPI flows into listed shares and bonds
Carry trades chasing the rate gap
Can leave within days when sentiment turns

body.text: A small current account deficit does not make the rupee safe. What matters is whether the gap is funded by stable money or hot money, and whether the capital account holds up when global investors turn nervous. A country with a 0.5% deficit and large FPI outflows can see more currency pressure than one with a 2% deficit funded by steady FDI.

children.text: Case Study: How India Escaped the Fragile Five

events.title: Deficit peaks
events.description: India's current account deficit reaches 4.8% of GDP, driven by high crude prices and record gold imports, with inflation also elevated.

events.title: Taper talk
events.description: The US Fed signals it may slow bond purchases. Hot money begins leaving emerging markets that rely on foreign funding.

events.title: Fragile Five and record low
events.description: India is grouped with the most vulnerable emerging economies. The rupee hits about 68.85 per dollar on 28 August.

events.title: Gold curbs
events.description: The government raises gold import duty in steps, reaching 10% in August, and introduces the 80:20 rule requiring 20% of gold imports to be re-exported.

events.title: RBI's FCNR(B) swap window
events.description: Under new Governor Raghuram Rajan, RBI offers banks concessional swaps on fresh NRI dollar deposits and foreign borrowings. The two windows draw in about $34 billion, around $26 billion of it through FCNR(B) deposits, and steady the rupee.

events.title: Deficit shrinks
events.description: The current account deficit falls to about 1.7% of GDP, and India drops out of the fragile group over the following years.

body.label: India's current account deficit, FY26
body.context: RBI data released in June 2026. The deficit was 0.6% of GDP in FY25 as well, and India even ran a $7.1 billion surplus in the January to March 2026 quarter.

body.title: Reading the macro dashboard
body.scenario: It is October. Brent crude has risen from $85 to $110 a barrel over three months. Gold imports are surging ahead of Dhanteras and the wedding season. India's latest CPI inflation print is 4.45% while US inflation is 3.4%. RBI data shows the current account deficit widened in the last quarter, and NSDL shows FPIs sold Indian shares heavily for six straight weeks. A friend says: "The current account deficit is only 0.5% of GDP, so the rupee will be fine."
body.prompt: Identify every force acting on the rupee in this scenario, sort them into current account, capital account and inflation effects, and explain what is wrong with your friend's reasoning.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Current account: higher crude prices and surging gold imports both widen the merchandise trade deficit, so India needs more dollars. The next quarter's deficit is likely to be larger than 0.5% of GDP.
2. Capital account: six weeks of heavy FPI selling means portfolio money is leaving and demanding dollars. This is hot money, and it can keep going.
3. Inflation: India's inflation is about one percentage point above US inflation. That supports gradual long-run rupee depreciation, but it is a slow effect, not the main driver this month.
4. Your friend is looking at a backward-looking number. The last reported deficit does not reflect the new oil and gold pressure, and it ignores the capital account entirely.
5. A small deficit funded by hot money can still produce a weak rupee when that money leaves, as the Q1 FY27 data showed. Watch monthly trade data, FPI flows and RBI's reserves, not just the quarterly current account figure.

body.title: Where FPI flows are recorded
body.textWithBlank: FDI, FPI flows and NRI deposits are recorded in the ___ account of the balance of payments.
body.explanation: Investment and borrowing flows belong to the capital, or financial, account. The current account covers trade in goods and services, investment income and transfers.

body.title: Inflation and the Balance of Payments

cards.definition: The idea that exchange rates adjust so identical goods cost the same across countries. Higher inflation implies long-run currency weakness.
Goods imports minus goods exports. India's is large because of crude oil, gold and electronics.
Goods and services trade, investment income and transfers such as remittances.
Investment and borrowing flows such as FDI, FPI, NRI deposits and foreign loans.
Current account plus capital account. The balance shows up as a change in forex reserves.
Short-term, fast-moving capital such as FPI and carry trade flows that can leave quickly.

points: Higher inflation erodes a currency's purchasing power. Relative PPP says the rupee should weaken by roughly the gap between Indian and US inflation over the long run.
PPP works over years, not months. Use it to understand drift, not to time trades.
The merchandise trade deficit is only part of the story. Services exports and remittances shrink India's current account deficit to a small fraction of the goods gap.
India's current account deficit was 0.6% of GDP in FY26, far below the 4.8% of FY13.
The capital account funds the deficit. In Q1 FY27, FPI outflows of $9.6 billion mattered more for the rupee than a $4.2 billion current account deficit.
Stable funding like FDI is safer than hot money like FPI flows, which can reverse quickly.
Crude oil and gold are the two biggest swing factors in India's external accounts.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Balance of payments data is from RBI releases as of the dates stated and is often revised. Some component figures are derived from published totals and may differ slightly from RBI's detailed tables. Worked examples on inflation and PPP are illustrative.
